headline_insight: Satisfaction is driven far more by country than by product: NPS across the three product lines varies by just 9.4 points (Crop 23.8, Health 16.6, Enhanced Credit Life 14.4), while country-level NPS spans 46.5 points, from Kenya at +36.2 to Tanzania at -10.3.
paragraphs: The product picture in this survey cannot be separated from the geographic one. Health Insurance accounts for 1,672 respondents, Enhanced Credit Life for 285 and Crop Insurance for 147 — and the Enhanced Credit Life and Crop Insurance counts map exactly onto Ghana (252 women, 33 men) and Vietnam (126 women, 21 men) respectively. Any statement about product performance is therefore also a statement about a single market's service delivery, and should be read that way. This confounding also explains the headline gender skew in product mix: 75.1% of female respondents hold Health Insurance against 90.8% of male respondents, while women are over-represented in Enhanced Credit Life (16.6% of women vs 5.6% of men, +11.0pp) and Crop Insurance (8.3% vs 3.6%, +4.7pp). These differences reflect where women sit in the portfolio geographically — Ghana (16.6% of women vs 5.6% of men) and Zambia (14.2% vs 11.4%) are female-weighted, while Uganda (10.5% vs 19.6%), Rwanda and Tanzania are male-weighted — rather than differential product uptake within a market.

Once that is understood, the most operationally useful finding is how flat the product-level NPS scores are relative to country scores. Crop Insurance leads on 23.8, Health Insurance sits at 16.6 and Enhanced Credit Life at 14.4 — a range of under ten points. By country, the spread is 46.5 points: Kenya (+36.2, n=265), Malawi (+32.4, n=275) and Zambia (+31.1, n=283) sit well above Vietnam (+23.8, n=147) and Ghana (+14.4, n=285), while Rwanda (+9.6), Uganda (+0.7) and Tanzania (-10.3) trail. Tanzania is the clear outlier, with 46.3% detractors — the highest of any country with an adequate sample — against 36.0% promoters. The LACRO markets (Bolivia, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Honduras with n=1 each, Mexico n=5) fail the minimum-sample gate and their NPS values, including the +100 and -100 extremes, should be disregarded as anything other than a record that responses were received. Benchmark data is not available for these NPS figures, so they should be read as an internal ranking rather than against any external standard. The implication is that improvement effort is better targeted at country-level distribution, claims handling and client communication — Tanzania, Uganda and Rwanda first — than at product redesign.

Within the product lines, three findings warrant attention. On Health Insurance, only 14.8% of women and 17.9% of men say insurance has made accessing medical care easier, while 42.9% of women say it has not and a further 42.3% report not having needed care; on out-of-pocket costs, 29.5% of women report costs lower or much lower, but 46.0% again fall into the not-applicable category. None of the gender gaps on these indicators reach significance after adjustment. This is less a gender-equity problem than a utilisation problem: a large share of the health-insured base has no experience of the product in use, which limits both perceived value and renewal logic. On Crop Insurance, only 2.4% of women and no men report recovering immediately or within a month after a shock, while 61.1% of women and 66.7% of men took more than three months — the payout is not arriving fast enough to function as a shock absorber. Directionally, women report more behavioural benefit than men (54.7% of women say their farming approach slightly or very much improved, against 28.6% of men, with 71.4% of men reporting no change), but with only 21 male respondents this comparison is illustrative, not robust, and should not be used as a basis for differentiated product claims.

The Enhanced Credit Life results contain the one set of statistically significant gender differences in this section, and they run in women's favour on awareness. Across the full sample, women are more likely than men to correctly identify that their credit life cover includes help with medical or hospital costs (15.7% vs 5.3%, +10.5pp, significant after adjustment), help when property or business assets are damaged (8.2% vs 2.7%) and help when crops or income are affected by weather (5.3% vs 0.9%). Women also rate the enhanced benefits more highly, with 64.3% calling them very valuable against 51.5% of men, though this gap is not significant. The critical read, however, is the absolute level rather than the gap: even among the Enhanced Credit Life holders themselves, 7.1% of women and 12.1% of men say they are not aware of the additional benefits at all, and portfolio-wide awareness of each specific benefit sits below 16%. Value that clients cannot name is value they cannot claim. No verbatim client quotes were captured for this section, so we cannot triangulate these patterns against client voice here; that is a gap worth closing in the next round, particularly in Tanzania and among Vietnam's crop clients, where the quantitative signal is either the weakest or the least statistically secure. For programming, the priorities are a Tanzania-focused service diagnostic, faster crop payout timelines, and a benefit-communication push at the point of loan disbursement so that Enhanced Credit Life's embedded benefits are understood before a shock, not after.
